findings.title: stdout_task panic silently zeroes all output via unwrap_or_default
findings.description: stdout_task.await.unwrap_or_default() silently swallows a JoinError (task panic) by replacing the entire result tuple with zero/empty defaults. If the task panics mid-stream the frontend never receives the terminal 'status:done' progress event (stuck streaming state) and the caller surfaces a misleading 'summarize call returned empty text' error with no indication of the real cause. Contrast with line 1791 where the stderr_task panic is properly logged. Any panic inside the spawned closure (serde error, OOM, etc.) is completely invisible.
findings.evidence:
let (summary, cost_usd, input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_read, cache_create, result_model) =
        stdout_task.await.unwrap_or_default();
findings.suggested_fix: Mirror the stderr_task pattern: stdout_task.await.unwrap_or_else(|e| { log::error!("summarize stdout task panicked: {e}"); Default::default() }). Also emit a terminal 'status:error' progress event from the error branch so the frontend can settle out of the streaming state.

findings.title: stderr drain task stops reading after cap — process can deadlock on wait()
findings.description: All three headless spawn helpers (enhance_prompt, generate_title, summarize_session) drain stderr in a tokio::spawn task that breaks out of the read loop once the accumulated buffer exceeds a cap (8 192 B for enhance/title, 32 KiB for summarize). After the break the task exits, dropping the BufReader and closing the read end of the pipe. If the child process subsequently tries to write more stderr than the OS pipe buffer can absorb (~64 KiB on Windows), it blocks in a write() syscall and never exits. The parent then calls child.wait().await (lines 1374, 1504, 1784) which waits for the process
findings.suggested_fix: Never break early from a drain loop. Either (a) keep reading to EOF but discard bytes beyond the cap (write into a fixed [u8; N] ring, or just read-and-discard after the cap), or (b) use tokio::io::copy with a sink after the limit: read into buf until cap, then tokio::io::copy(&mut remaining_reader, &mut tokio::io::sink()).await. Both keep the pipe drained so the child can exit. Pattern: `while let Ok(Some(l)) = lines.next_line().await { if buf.len() < CAP { buf.push_str(&l); buf.push('\n'); } }

findings.title: stdout drain task panic silently replaced with zero defaults
findings.description: In assistant_summarize_session, the stdout drain task (which accumulates summary text, cost, tokens, and model) is awaited with `.unwrap_or_default()`. A panic in that task is completely silent — no log, no error propagation. All accumulated data is replaced with empty string / 0 / None defaults. The code then hits `if summary.is_empty()` and returns a generic 'summarize call returned empty text' error, discarding the actual panic cause entirely. By contrast, the stderr task at line 1791 at least logs the panic. The asymmetry means the most important drain task (stdout) has weaker failure hand
findings.evidence:
let (summary, cost_usd, input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_read, cache_create, result_model) =
        stdout_task.await.unwrap_or_default();
findings.suggested_fix: Mirror the stderr pattern: `stdout_task.await.unwrap_or_else(|e| { log::error!("summarize stdout drain task panicked: {e}"); Default::default() })`, or propagate the JoinError as a command error so the caller sees the real failure rather than a misleading empty-output message.

findings.title: Leaked stdout_task and stderr_task on child.wait() error path
findings.description: stdout_task (spawned at line 2645) and stderr_task (spawned at line 2754) are both live by the time the reap loop starts at line 2787. If child.wait() returns Err, the function returns early at line 2790 via `return Err(format!("await claude: {e}"))` without reaching the abort/timeout block at lines 2827-2845. Both tasks continue running indefinitely: stdout_task holds stdin (keeping the child's stdin pipe open) and reads stdout; stderr_task reads stderr. These tasks can only terminate when the child process eventually closes its pipe ends — which may never happen if the child is already in an

findings.suggested_fix: Before the early return, abort both tasks: `stdout_task.abort(); stderr_task.abort();`. A drop-guard (e.g. a scopeguard or RAII wrapper) is more robust so other early returns added in future are covered automatically.

findings.title: Claude subprocess spawned with --permission-mode bypassPermissions for transcript cleanup
findings.description: Every cleanup invocation spawns `claude -p --permission-mode bypassPermissions`. bypassPermissions disables all tool-use permission gates for the spawned Claude process. The user's raw speech transcript is piped in as the user-turn content. If a user speaks content that resembles a Claude instruction (or if an attacker can influence what the user says / what appears in the transcript), the subprocess has unrestricted tool access — it can read arbitrary files, run shell commands, etc. — with no confirmation prompt. The -p/pipe mode is designed for trusted scripted use; bypassPermissions on atta
findings.evidence:
.arg("--permission-mode")
        .arg("bypassPermissions")
findings.suggested_fix: Use --permission-mode default (or omit the flag) so the spawned Claude CLI applies normal tool-permission gates. Alternatively restrict the invocation to a read-only permission set. The cleanup task only needs to read stdin and write stdout; it should never need file-system or shell tools, so also pass --no-tools or an allowlist of zero tools if the CLI supports it.

findings.title: Blocking std::sync::mpsc::recv() on tokio worker thread inside async fn
findings.description: stt_start_recording is a #[tauri::command] async fn that runs on a tokio worker thread. Line 388 calls cap_ready_rx.recv() — a std::sync::mpsc blocking receive — directly on the tokio runtime without spawn_blocking. If mic capture initialisation takes any time (device open, WASAPI negotiation), this parks the worker thread, starving other tokio tasks on that thread. On a single-threaded tokio runtime it would deadlock entirely, and even on multi-threaded runtimes it can exhaust the thread pool under concurrent load.
findings.suggested_fix: Wrap the blocking receive in tokio::task::spawn_blocking: `let ring = tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || cap_ready_rx.recv()).await.map_err(...)?.map_err(...)?;` This keeps the tokio worker free while the capture thread initialises the device.

findings.title: JoinHandle from rolling_window_loop task dropped without join — leaked task races with next session
findings.description: tokio::spawn returns a JoinHandle that is immediately dropped (not stored anywhere). The rolling-window task is expected to stop via the CancellationToken, but stt_stop_recording only calls shutdown_capture() which cancels the token and returns immediately — it never awaits the spawned task's completion. Until the task actually observes cancel.cancelled() and returns, it continues to call audio::peek_window and spawn_blocking transcribe jobs against the ring and engine that may already be in use by the final-transcription path in stt_stop_recording. A rapid stop+start sequence can result in tw
findings.suggested_fix: Store the JoinHandle in ActiveSession alongside rolling_cancel. In shutdown_capture (or in stt_stop_recording after shutdown_capture), abort or await the handle before draining the ring for final transcription: `if let Some(h) = self.rolling_task.take() { h.abort(); let _ = h.await; }`

findings.title: tool_grep: no per-file size cap before full read — unbounded allocation
findings.description: tool_grep reads each file fully into memory (std::fs::read) with no size limit. MAX_READ_BYTES (500 KB) is enforced only in tool_read_file. A large non-binary file (e.g. a multi-GB log or generated file) that passes the 8-KiB NUL probe will be loaded in full. With MAX_GREP_FILES=5000 and no cap, a single grep call can exhaust process memory.
findings.suggested_fix: After the binary probe block, stat the file and skip if its size exceeds a threshold (e.g. MAX_READ_BYTES or a dedicated MAX_GREP_FILE_BYTES constant) before calling std::fs::read. Alternatively, reuse the already-opened probe File: seek back to 0 and read up to the cap, avoiding the second open entirely.

findings.title: UTF-8 line truncation at byte offset 200 can panic on multi-byte codepoints

If a multi-byte UTF-8 codepoint spans bytes 199-200 (e.g. a 2-byte sequence starting at byte 199), this panics with 'byte index 200 is not a char boundary'. The file is proven valid UTF-8 (line 295 uses `from_utf8`) so any UTF-8 char wider than 1 byte near position 200 triggers the panic and crashes the MCP server subprocess.

findings.title: Absolute paths with `..` components bypass traversal guard
findings.description: The `..` component check at line 83 is inside the `else if` branch that only runs for relative paths. For absolute paths the code jumps to the `starts_with(root)` check at line 74, which uses lexical prefix comparison. An absolute path containing `..` (e.g. `/workspace/../workspace/../../etc/passwd`) passes `starts_with` if the string happens to start with the root prefix but resolves outside it. The ParentDir guard is never reached for absolute paths, so path-traversal through an absolute input is possible.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a `ParentDir` component check for absolute paths too, before the `starts_with` test. Or canonicalize both root and the joined path with `std::fs::canonicalize` (if existence is acceptable) or use a lexical normalization that collapses `..` segments before the prefix comparison.

findings.title: SHA-256 integrity check silently skipped on resumed downloads
findings.description: The hasher is set to None whenever resume_from > 0 (line 198-202). If a .partial file already exists on disk — whether from a prior interrupted download or from an attacker/malware writing a crafted partial — the entire SHA-256 verification branch (lines 239-251) is skipped because hasher is None. The corrupted/tampered bytes are never hashed, and the partial is renamed to the final path unconditionally at line 253. Since sha256 entries are now populated in the catalogue (lines 45-66), this is a live bypass: a malicious .partial will pass the check that was supposed to catch it.
findings.suggested_fix: On resume, hash only the newly-received bytes but that cannot reconstruct the full-file hash. The correct fix is to either (a) re-hash the on-disk partial before appending (read it back through a Sha256 instance, then continue streaming), or (b) on a sha256-pinned entry with resume_from > 0, refuse to resume and force a fresh download (`resume_from = 0`, truncate). Option (b) is simpler and safe given that these are one-time model downloads.

findings.title: auto-detect language path silently clobbered
findings.description: The public API documents `language: None` as whisper.cpp auto-detect, but `language.or(Some("en"))` unconditionally substitutes `"en"` for `None`. No caller can ever reach the auto-detect code path; the documented contract is silently broken.
findings.evidence: params.set_language(language.or(Some("en")));
findings.suggested_fix: Pass `language` directly: `params.set_language(language);`. If a hard English default is desired, document it in the param signature and remove the `None`-means-auto-detect doc comment, or expose a separate `auto_detect: bool` flag.

findings.title: Child process orphaned on timeout — not killed before drop
findings.description: When the 15-second timeout fires, the function returns immediately without calling child.kill() or child.wait(). The tokio::process::Child is then dropped. On Unix, dropping a Child without waiting leaves a zombie; on Windows it leaks the process handle and the claude subprocess keeps running (consuming CPU/memory/network), holding the stdout/stderr pipes open. Each STT cleanup that times out spawns a persistent orphan. Over a session with repeated timeouts this accumulates into multiple dangling claude -p processes.
findings.suggested_fix: Before returning in the timeout arm, kill and reap the child: `let _ = child.kill().await; let _ = child.wait().await; return Ok(raw.to_string());`. Alternatively, wrap the whole child lifetime in a guard that calls kill+wait on drop.

findings.title: No URL scheme validation — file:// and javascript: URLs accepted
findings.description: parse_url only checks syntactic validity; it accepts any scheme. A caller passing a file:// URL loads arbitrary local files in the embedded child WebView2 (full filesystem read with no sandbox boundary because child webviews share the host origin context). A javascript: URL executes arbitrary JS in the webview. Both vectors are reachable from the IPC-exposed open/navigate Tauri commands that delegate here.

findings.title: No URL scheme allowlist — file://, javascript:, data: accepted by browser_open / browser_navigate
findings.description: Both browser_open and browser_navigate receive a raw url: String from the frontend IPC and pass it directly to parse_url(), which only checks syntactic validity. Schemes such as file://, javascript:, data:, and blob: are syntactically valid and will be accepted, then forwarded to wv.navigate() on the embedded child WebView2. A compromised renderer or malicious workspace content could navigate the dock webview to local filesystem paths (file://C:/...) or execute arbitrary JavaScript (javascript:...) inside the trusted child webview context.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a scheme allowlist in parse_url() (or a new validate_url() called before open/navigate): reject anything whose scheme is not http or https. Example: if !matches!(u.scheme(), "http" | "https") { return Err(format!("disallowed scheme '{}'", u.scheme())); }

findings.title: Command injection via unsanitized `path` passed through `cmd /C code <path>`
findings.description: On Windows, `path` (a raw frontend-supplied string) is passed as a positional arg to `cmd /C code <path>`. `cmd.exe` with `/C` tokenizes its trailing arguments as a command line, meaning shell metacharacters in `path` (e.g. `& calc`, `| whoami`, `; rm ...`) are interpreted by cmd.exe before VS Code ever sees them. A malicious workspace path or a path returned from an MCP tool that includes `&`, `|`, `>`, or `&&` can inject and execute arbitrary commands with the app's privileges.
findings.evidence: c.args(["/C", "code", &path]);
findings.suggested_fix: Avoid routing through `cmd /C`. Instead, resolve `code.cmd` explicitly (e.g. search `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Microsoft VS Code\bin\code.cmd`) and invoke it directly via `Command::new(resolved_code_cmd).arg(&path)`, keeping the path as a separate argument so no shell tokenization occurs. Alternatively, use `std::process::Command::new("cmd").arg("/C").arg("code").arg(&path)` which passes `path` as a discrete argv element — but only if cmd.exe honours argv[] boundaries with `/C` (it does not reliab

The tooltip (use:tooltip) is not exposed to the accessibility tree.

findings.title: Missing return after Task/Agent block — falls through to activity label + ToolChip append
findings.description: appendToolUse() has explicit `return` statements after TodoWrite, TaskCreate, and TaskUpdate blocks, but the Task/Agent branch (lines 599-606) has no `return`. Execution continues to line 607-614: the DENY check (ToolSearch only) passes for Task/Agent, so `this.activity.currentLabel` is set AND `mutateStreaming` appends a ToolChip to the streaming message. This double-processes Task/Agent tool calls — they both push to `agentSpawns` AND produce a rendered tool chip — which is inconsistent with the pattern for every other internal tool name and likely wrong.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `return;` at line 606 immediately after the closing `}` of the Task/Agent block, the same way TodoWrite/TaskCreate/TaskUpdate each return early. If Task/Agent calls should also produce a ToolChip, the intent should be documented; otherwise the fall-through is a bug.

findings.title: applyTaskCreate generates numeric IDs incompatible with applyTodoWrite's content-keyed IDs

If a session uses both APIs — TaskCreate builds tasks "1","2","3", then TodoWrite fires and replaces the array — a subsequent applyTaskUpdate("2") finds no match (no task has id "2" anymore) and silently no-ops. The two sub-APIs share `this.tasks` but use incompatible ID schemes with no guard against cross-contamination, so task status updates are silently
findings.suggested_fix: Give TaskCreate IDs the same numeric-string format as the CLI's taskId but ensure they survive a TodoWrite. Either: (a) reset tasks entirely when switching between the two APIs and accept the incompatibility is by design, or (b) use a shared ID-generation scheme (e.g., monotonic counter on TabState) so TaskUpdate can always find the right task regardless of whether TodoWrite has fired. At minimum, add a guard in applyTodoWrite that resets numeric-ID tasks when the incoming todos list comes from

findings.title: applyTaskCreate assigns IDs from total tasks.length, breaking applyTaskUpdate
findings.description: applyTaskCreate generates task IDs using `String(this.tasks.length + 1)`, treating the shared `tasks` array length as a 1-based creation counter. If a prior TodoWrite call has populated tasks (with ids like 'todo-buy milk'), the first TaskCreate task gets id '3' (not '1'). The CLI's TaskUpdate.taskId is 1-based relative to TaskCreate-only order. applyTaskUpdate at line 567 matches by `t.id === taskId`, so when CLI sends `{ taskId: '1' }` it finds nothing and silently no-ops. All task-status updates are silently dropped whenever TodoWrite and TaskCreate are mixed.
findings.evidence:
const id = String(this.tasks.length + 1);
this.tasks = [...this.tasks, { id, content: subject, status: "pending" }];
findings.suggested_fix: Track a separate `taskCreateCount` field on TabState (initialized to 0, incremented only in applyTaskCreate) and use `String(this.taskCreateCount + 1)` as the id. Reset alongside `tasks` on clearConversation / compaction. This makes the numeric index match the CLI's 1-based creation order regardless of how many TodoWrite tasks coexist.

findings.title: Six config set* mutators leave invoke() errors unhandled — state silently diverges from backend
findings.description: setApiKey (1734), setUseFullConfig (1741), setMaxBudgetUsd (1746), setTrustLevel (1752), setAutoCompactThreshold (1757), and setCompactModel (1763) all `await invoke(...)` with no try/catch. If the backend call throws, the in-memory state mutation on the very next line is skipped, so the UI shows the old value while the backend was never actually updated — or the reverse. The rejection propagates to callers in SettingsPage that typically call these with `void` or no `.catch()`, so the error is silently dropped. Violates the fail-loud rule and leaves frontend/backend config in diverged state.
findings.suggested_fix: Wrap each mutator body in try/catch. On catch, surface the error via a toast or `this.lastNotice` and do NOT apply the state mutation. Pattern: `try { await invoke(...); this.field = v; } catch (e) { this.lastNotice = String(e); throw e; }`. The rethrow keeps callers that do await them informed.

findings.title: Tooltip string literal contains un-interpolated Svelte expression
findings.description: The pane-badge tooltip is written as a plain JS string with curly braces: `{"Open in pane {paneIndexFor(id)}"}`. Curly braces inside a JS string literal are not Svelte template expressions — they are never evaluated. The tooltip always renders the literal text `Open in pane {paneIndexFor(id)}` rather than the actual pane number.
findings.evidence: <span class="pane-badge" use:tooltip={"Open in pane {paneIndexFor(id)}"}>
findings.suggested_fix: Use a template literal so the expression is evaluated: use:tooltip={`Open in pane ${paneIndexFor(id)}`}

findings.title: expandedThinking keyed by unstable grouped[] index — wrong block expanded after streaming recompute
findings.description: The `expandedThinking` Set is indexed by `bi`, which is `ui` — the position of a unit inside the `grouped` derived array (line 786). `grouped` is a `$derived` that recomputes every time `message.blocks` changes during streaming: new tool blocks arrive, prose segments split, toolgroups coalesce. Each recompute shifts every `ui` value. A thinking block that was at grouped index 2 becomes index 3 once an earlier tool block is inserted, so `expandedThinking.has(2)` now resolves against whatever block landed at position 2 rather than the originally toggled thinking block. The user clicks to expand
findings.suggested_fix: Key expandedThinking by a stable identity instead of a positional index. For thinking blocks, use a block-level id if one exists on the Block type, or use the `unit.key` string (e.g. `b_3`) which is computed once from the raw block position at grouping time and does not shift. Pass `unit.key` (or a derived stable string) as the `bi` argument for single-block nodes and derive a similarly stable key for toolgroup inner blocks.

findings.title: askSubmitting never reset on success — submit/cancel buttons permanently stuck
findings.description: submitAskUser and cancelAskUser both set askSubmitting = true before the IPC await, but only reset it in the catch block. On a successful IPC call (no exception thrown) askSubmitting stays true forever. The disabled binding at line 687 reads `!askCanSubmit || askSubmitting || !askRequestId`, so if tool.status does not transition to 'done' promptly (e.g. a backend race or dropped event), the submit and cancel buttons are permanently disabled with no recovery path and no timeout.
findings.evidence: disabled={!askCanSubmit || askSubmitting || !askRequestId}
findings.suggested_fix: Add a finally block in both submitAskUser and cancelAskUser that resets askSubmitting = false unless askAnswered is already true. E.g.: try { await assistant.submitAskUserAnswer(...) } catch (e) { ... askSubmitting = false; } finally { if (!askAnswered) askSubmitting = false; } — or reset unconditionally and rely on askAnswered to gate the UI.

findings.title: submitAskUser / cancelAskUser errors swallowed silently — no user-visible feedback on IPC failure
findings.description: The Submit (line 688) and Dismiss (line 683) buttons invoke `submitAskUser` / `cancelAskUser`, which catch IPC errors with only `console.warn` and reset `askSubmitting`. If the Tauri invoke fails (e.g. the chat session is gone), the ask-body renders no error message — the form silently returns to the editable state with no explanation. This violates the project's "fail loud, never fake" rule and leaves users unable to distinguish a transient retry from a permanent failure.
findings.suggested_fix: Introduce a local `$state askError = $state<string | null>(null)` reactive variable. In the catch blocks, set `askError` to a short message (e.g. `"Failed to send — please retry"`) and render it near the action buttons. Clear it on the next successful submit attempt.

findings.title: openTab called as side-effect of right-click context menu
findings.description: onRowContext calls assistant.openTab(id) whenever the right-clicked conversation is not already in openTabs, before showing the context menu. This switches/opens the tab — a user-visible side effect — purely from a right-click intended only to open a menu. Users right-clicking to inspect a conversation without opening it will have it forced open regardless of what they pick in the menu (or even if they dismiss it).
findings.suggested_fix: Remove the openTab call from onRowContext entirely. Let the context menu items themselves decide whether to open the tab (e.g. an 'Open' action inside OpenInPaneMenu). Set ctxMenu unconditionally: `ctxMenu = { tabId: id, x: e.clientX, y: e.clientY };`

findings.title: Unhandled rejection from openTab silently swallowed in onRowContext
findings.description: onRowContext calls `void assistant.openTab(id).then(...)` with no .catch(). If openTab rejects (e.g. backend error), the rejection is silently dropped, the context menu never appears, and the user gets no feedback. Using `void` discards the Promise entirely, including any rejection.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a .catch() handler: `void assistant.openTab(id).then(() => { ctxMenu = {...} }).catch(err => console.error('openTab failed', err))`, or use try/catch inside an async IIFE so errors surface visibly rather than being silently swallowed.

Alternatively restrict with `ALLOWED_STYLE_ATTR: [

findings.title: Per-turn DOM parse + TreeWalker in $derived runs on every shownCount tick (~24 fps) during streaming
findings.description: The `processed` $derived calls `revealWords(baseHtml, shownCount)` on every change to `shownCount`, which the rAF loop in the $effect advances at WORD_MS=42ms (~24 fps). `revealWords` creates a `<template>` element, sets `.innerHTML` (full HTML parse), creates a TreeWalker, walks all text nodes, and serializes back via `.innerHTML`. For a long assistant response with hundreds of words, this is a full DOM parse + serialize at 24 fps for the entire duration of the streaming animation. The `parsed` $derived correctly caches the markdown→HTML step, but `processed` re-does the expensive DOM walk ev
findings.suggested_fix: Cache the TreeWalker word-split as a list of (textNode-path, words[]) tuples derived from `parsed` alone, then on each `shownCount` tick only mutate span classNames/visibility on an already-built fragment rather than reparsing HTML. Alternatively, switch to a pure-CSS counter approach: emit all words as `.md-w-hold` spans in the `parsed` pass, then use a CSS custom property `--shown` updated by the rAF loop to control which spans are visible — eliminating per-tick DOM parsing entirely.

findings.title: Undeclared `opener` causes ReferenceError at runtime
findings.description: `openSource` calls `opener.openUrl(item.value)` but `opener` is never imported, declared as `$state`, or otherwise defined in the script block. In a browser context `window.opener` is a `Window | null` (and would be `null` in a Tauri WebView) and has no `.openUrl` method. Any invocation of `openSource` for a URL will throw `ReferenceError: opener is not defined` (or crash on `.openUrl` being undefined) at runtime. The Sources panel that would call this function appears to be planned but not yet rendered in the template — however the function and bug are live in the shipped file.
findings.suggested_fix: Import the Tauri shell/opener plugin and declare it: `import { open as openUrl } from '@tauri-apps/plugin-shell'` (or `@tauri-apps/plugin-opener` in Tauri 2). Replace `opener.openUrl(item.value)` with `await openUrl(item.value)` and remove the `if (!opener) return` guard.

findings.title: opener is undefined — openSource always silently no-ops
findings.description: The `opener` identifier is never imported or declared anywhere in the file. The guard `if (!opener) return` at line 253 evaluates to `if (undefined) return`, so `openSource` always returns early without opening the URL or copying the query. The feature is completely dead and fails silently — violating the fail-loud rule. The sibling files (Markdown.svelte, FilePathMenu.svelte) correctly import from `@tauri-apps/plugin-opener`.
findings.evidence:
if (!opener) return;
      if (item.kind === "url") await opener.openUrl(item.value);
findings.suggested_fix: Add `import { openUrl } from "@tauri-apps/plugin-opener";` at the top of the script block and replace `opener.openUrl(item.value)` with the direct `openUrl(item.value)` call, removing the dead `opener` guard. Also surface errors rather than swallowing them (or at minimum promote the `console.warn` to `console.error`).

findings.title: Whisper stop() silently no-ops during recording start-up race
findings.description: For the Whisper engine, `recording` is only set to `true` when the async `stt://state: recording` event arrives (line 191), NOT inside `start()` (line 297 comment confirms this). `stop()` at line 340 guards with `if (!this.recording && !this.transcribing) return this.lastTranscript` — so any call to `stop()` in the window between `stt_start_recording` returning and the state event firing silently returns an empty transcript without actually invoking `stt_stop_recording`. The recording continues until the backend times out or is killed externally, and the caller gets no feedback.
findings.evidence: if (!this.recording && !this.transcribing) return this.lastTranscript;
findings.suggested_fix: For Whisper, call `invoke('stt_stop_recording')` unconditionally (or track a separate `startInvoked` flag set synchronously in `start()` before the event arrives), so `stop()` can honour requests during the startup race window.

findings.title: Auto-expand heuristic always returns 1 for any non-identical strings, making SMALL_DIFF threshold useless
findings.description: The changed-line count used to decide auto-expand is computed as Math.abs(oldLines.length - newLines.length) + (oldStr === newStr ? 0 : 1). For any two strings that differ but have the same line count (e.g. replacing 50 lines with 50 different lines), this evaluates to 0 + 1 = 1, which is always <= SMALL_DIFF (12). The component therefore auto-expands every non-trivially-large diff regardless of actual change size, defeating the intent of hiding large diffs behind the chevron.
findings.suggested_fix: Count the actual number of changed lines from the diff chunks, or approximate with a line-level comparison: sum the lengths of all removed and added arrays from diffArrays(oldLines, newLines). E.g.: const chunks = diffArrays(oldLines.split('\n'), newStr.split('\n')); const changed = chunks.reduce((n,c) => c.added || c.removed ? n + c.value.length : n, 0); return changed <= SMALL_DIFF;

findings.title: Focus outline suppressed on buttons with no replacement
findings.description: `.cp-item:focus-visible { outline: none }` removes the browser's default focus ring on command-palette buttons without providing a custom replacement. Arrow-key navigation sets `activeIdx` (and thus `data-active`) via `onmouseenter`/keyboard, but a user who tabs directly into the list gets no visible focus indicator — the `data-active` style is only applied when `idx === activeIdx`, not on native `:focus-visible`. WCAG 2.4.11 (Focus Appearance) requires a visible focus indicator.
findings.evidence: .cp-item:focus-visible { outline: none; }
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the blanket `outline: none` with a custom ring that matches the active style, e.g. `.cp-item:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid var(--accent); outline-offset: -2px; }`. This preserves keyboard discoverability while keeping the custom look.

findings.title: Each-block keyed by index instead of stable pane identity
findings.description: The {#each} loop over `assistant.panes` uses the loop index `i` as the keying expression `(i)`. Svelte uses the key to decide which existing component instance maps to which list entry. When a pane is removed from the middle, or panes are reordered, index-keying causes Svelte to hand an existing `AssistantPane` instance the props of the wrong pane (the one that shifted into its slot) rather than destroying the old instance and mounting a fresh one. Internal state held by `AssistantPane` (scroll position, local `$state`, focus, etc.) will bleed across the wrong tab. The fix is to key by the sta
findings.evidence: {#each assistant.panes as p, i (i)}
findings.suggested_fix: Change `(i)` to `(p.tabId ?? i)` — or, if tabId is always set for rendered panes, simply `(p.tabId)`. This ensures a pane's DOM/component instance is destroyed and re-created when its identity changes, not recycled into a sibling slot.

findings.title: Partial delete + unconditional state wipe in deleteAllConversations
findings.description: The try/catch wraps the entire delete loop (lines 306-308). If any invoke fails mid-loop, the catch fires and sets lastError — but execution falls through to the unconditional state-wipe block (lines 314-321) regardless. The remaining conversations are not deleted from disk, yet every open tab is dropped and all active-convo fields are nulled. This leaves the UI in a fully-cleared state while orphaned conversation records remain on disk, with no way for the user to recover without restarting.
findings.suggested_fix: Either (a) move the state-wipe inside the try block so it only runs on full success, or (b) collect per-id errors and only wipe tabs for successfully-deleted ids. Also consider Promise.allSettled to attempt all deletes before deciding what to wipe. Example: move lines 314-321 inside the try block after the loop so a partial failure aborts the wipe.

findings.title: refreshConversations silently swallows IPC errors with no user-visible signal
findings.description: refreshConversations catches all invoke errors and logs only to console.warn, never surfacing them to host.lastError or any UI-visible field. This is called after every save, rename, delete, and title-generation pass. A persistent IPC failure (e.g. backend crash) leaves host.conversations stale with no indication to the user — the conversation list silently shows outdated data. Violates the project's fail-loud rule.
findings.suggested_fix: Surface persistent failures: set host.lastError = `Failed to refresh conversations: ${String(e)}` inside the catch, or re-throw and let each call-site decide. At minimum the user should see a notice when the list can't be updated after a mutating operation.

findings.title: Orphan boundary block left in messages when listen() rejects
findings.description: The staged boundary message is appended to tab.messages at line 143 before the try block begins at line 161. If the await listen(...) call at line 162 rejects (IPC error, event system unavailable), execution jumps directly to the finally block, which only resets compactingNow and calls progressUnlisten() (null-safe). The orphaned boundary ChatMessage with streaming: true remains permanently in the chat — it is never cleaned up. The two explicit cleanup paths (lines 174 and 185) are inside the try body and are never reached.
findings.suggested_fix: Move the stagedBoundary push inside the try block (after the listen() call succeeds), or add a cleanup guard in the finally block: if (tab.messages.some(m => m.id === boundaryId) && !res_succeeded) { tab.messages = tab.messages.filter(m => m.id !== boundaryId); }. A simpler approach is to wrap the entire stagedBoundary setup + listen() in the try and remove the boundary in the finally when the operation did not succeed.

findings.title: browser_show IPC rejection silently swallowed — fail-loud violation
findings.description: Inside the $effect visibility handler, invoke("browser_show") is called with void and a .then(syncBounds) but no .catch(). If the command fails (native webview not ready, Tauri error, etc.), the rejection is unhandled: the native webview remains hidden, syncBounds never runs, and the user gets no error feedback. This violates the project fail-loud rule and makes the browser appear to silently freeze.
findings.evidence: void invoke("browser_show").then(syncBounds);
findings.suggested_fix: Add a .catch handler: `void invoke("browser_show").then(syncBounds).catch((e) => { error = String(e); });` — surfaces the failure in the existing error display rather than dropping it.

findings.title: pause/resume resets full timeout instead of preserving remaining time
findings.description: onmouseenter calls toast.pause(id) which clears the timer; onmouseleave calls toast.resume(id) which always schedules a NEW full-duration timeout (e.g. 4000ms for info). A toast hovered at T=3900ms gets its countdown silently reset to T+4000ms on mouseleave — it stays visible far longer than the user expects and, in a stress scenario where the user moves the mouse in/out repeatedly, accumulates resets indefinitely. The store has no concept of elapsed time.
findings.evidence:
onmouseenter={() => toast.pause(item.id)}
onmouseleave={() => toast.resume(item.id)}
findings.suggested_fix: Track the timer start timestamp alongside the setTimeout handle in ToastStore. On pause, record `elapsed = Date.now() - startedAt`. On resume, schedule `setTimeout(dismiss, remaining)` where `remaining = totalMs - elapsed`. This preserves the original expiry intent.

findings.title: Enter key always confirms regardless of focused element
findings.description: onKey binds to svelte:window and fires decide(true) on Enter unconditionally. When the user tabs focus to the Cancel button, the checkbox, or any element outside the dialog overlay, pressing Enter still calls onClose({confirmed:true}). This can trigger destructive actions (isDanger=true paths) when the user intends to cancel or dismiss.
findings.evidence: if (e.key === "Enter") decide(true);
findings.suggested_fix: Guard with a focus check: only confirm if the confirm button (or the dialog shell) holds focus. E.g. add a ref to the confirm button and check `document.activeElement === confirmBtn` before calling decide(true), or restrict to `e.key === 'Enter' && document.activeElement?.closest('.dialog-shell')`.

findings.title: opener:allow-open-url wildcard reachable from AI-generated markdown links
findings.description: opener:allow-open-url permits http://** and https://** with no domain restriction. Markdown.svelte intercepts every anchor click inside assistant replies and calls openUrl(href) with the raw href string — no scheme or domain filter. A malicious or compromised workspace file (e.g., a README whose content is returned in a tool response) can embed any link, which the assistant renders and the user may click, triggering openUrl to launch an arbitrary URL in the default browser. In a pure-local assistant there is no legitimate need to open arbitrary http/https URLs that the AI suggests; restricting
findings.suggested_fix: Restrict the allow list to only the domains the app genuinely needs to open: the GitHub releases page for self-update (https://github.com/**) and remove http://** entirely. If the activity panel / chat must support arbitrary user-clicked URLs, gate the call behind explicit user intent UI rather than auto-opening on any anchor click from AI-generated content.

findings.title: Unvalidated releaseUrl opened via openUrl() without scheme/host check
findings.description: openReleasePage() takes updates.info.releaseUrl (sourced from the GitHub API's html_url field) and passes it directly to openUrl() with no scheme or host validation. A spoofed or MitM'd API response could supply any URL — including file://, javascript:, or a phishing https:// domain — and it will be opened in the user's default browser. The download_update command has an explicit starts_with host check (lines 167–169 of update.rs), but this companion code path has none.
findings.suggested_fix: Before calling openUrl, assert the URL starts with 'https://github.com/': `if (!url.startsWith('https://github.com/')) return;`. Alternatively, reconstruct the URL from the validated version tag instead of echoing the API value.

findings.title: assistant_set_thinking_effort / assistant_set_permission_mode registered but never invoked — dual-storage split
findings.description: The backend registers and validates `assistant_set_thinking_effort` and `assistant_set_permission_mode` (plus their matching `_get_*` counterparts) and persists them to the Rust config file. The frontend never calls any of these four commands. Instead it stores both values exclusively in localStorage via `loadEffort()`/`saveEffort()` and `loadPermissionMode()`/`savePermissionMode()`. Per-turn values are passed directly as params to `assistant_send`. The two storage systems are completely disconnected: a backend config-file change has zero UI effect; a localStorage reset (WebView2 profile wipe,
findings.suggested_fix: Pick one storage layer. Easiest: on settings load call `assistant_get_thinking_effort` and `assistant_get_permission_mode` to seed state (replacing localStorage reads), and on change call the IPC setters instead of `saveEffort`/`savePermissionMode`. This removes the localStorage fallback entirely and makes the Rust config file authoritative. Alternatively, remove the four backend commands and keep localStorage-only (simpler, but loses config-file persistence for these two fields).

findings.title: API key plaintext disk fallback survives failed keychain migration
findings.description: current_api_key() falls back to loading the raw api_key field from config.json when the keychain entry is absent. If the one-shot migration in load_config() fails (keychain unavailable, e.g. headless, locked session, first-boot race), the key is never cleared from the JSON file and is re-read in plaintext from disk on every CLI spawn. The field is marked skip_serializing_if=Option::is_none, so save_config() will not re-write it — but the migration failure path at line 666 explicitly skips the save, leaving the plaintext value resident indefinitely.
findings.suggested_fix: On successful keychain migration, zero out and overwrite the config.json field unconditionally (not only on save_config success). On migration failure, do not fall back silently — surface a persistent warning to the user and refuse to use the plaintext key, or at minimum log::warn with the actual key slot name so the operator knows the plaintext path is active.

findings.title: validate_path absolute-path branch bypasses `..` check — workspace escape via git_diff / git_commit
findings.description: The absolute-path branch of validate_path (lines 72-76) only calls p.starts_with(root). Rust's PathBuf::starts_with does component-prefix matching and returns true for paths that contain .. components above the root, e.g. /workspace/a/../../etc/passwd starts_with /workspace = true even though it resolves outside. The relative-path branch correctly rejects ParentDir components (line 83) but the absolute-path branch has no equivalent guard. Callers: tool_git_diff (path param) and tool_git_commit (paths array) both feed user-supplied absolute paths through this function and then pass the raw (unr

findings.title: Compaction state machine: forceNextFirstTurn not persisted — post-restart regression sends --resume on a non-existent JSONL
findings.description: After compactConversation() succeeds it sets tab.convoCreatedAt = null (line 209) and tab.forceNextFirstTurn = true (line 210) then immediately calls scheduleSave(true) (line 228). doSave() in persistence.ts line 156 unconditionally writes tab.convoCreatedAt = record.createdAt (buildSaveRecord falls back to Date.now() when null), so convoCreatedAt is non-null again before the awaited save resolves. forceNextFirstTurn is in-memory only — never written to the ConversationRecord. On any restart (crash, reload, window close) before the first post-compaction send(), forceNextFirstTurn resets to fal
findings.suggested_fix: Persist forceNextFirstTurn (or an equivalent isPostCompaction flag) in ConversationRecord and re-hydrate it in the loader. Alternatively, derive first-turn from the absence of a JSONL file on disk rather than in-memory flags. A regression test should: (1) run compactConversation on a mock host, (2) simulate a page reload by re-hydrating tab state from the persisted record, (3) call send() and assert that isFirstTurn is true and cliSessionId matches the reminted newSid.

findings.title: Unsanitized path from disk used as CLI working directory
findings.description: load_session_cwd reads a PathBuf from a sidecar file under ~/.rift/assistant/sessions/ and returns it with no validation — no canonicalization, no prefix check against known workspace roots. The returned value is subsequently passed as current_dir() when spawning the claude CLI subprocess. If the sidecar file is tampered with (writable by any process running as the same user, or via a symlink/rename race), an attacker can steer the CLI spawn into an arbitrary directory, changing which CLAUDE.md/.mcp.json/workspace tools the CLI picks up — effectively selecting a malicious workspace.
findings.suggested_fix: After reading, canonicalize the path with std::fs::canonicalize and verify it is_dir(). Optionally cross-check it against the set of paths the user explicitly opened as workspace roots (recent_roots / current_root from AssistantConfig) before accepting it as a spawn cwd.

findings.title: Full filesystem path leaked in IPC error return
findings.description: assistant_load_conversation returns a Tauri IPC error string containing the full on-disk path (including the user's home directory) via p.display(). This string is returned to the frontend and can be surfaced in UI error toasts or developer console logs, leaking the host filesystem layout (home dir, ~/.rift path) to any renderer-side code or an XSS payload.
findings.evidence: let bytes = std::fs::read(&p).map_err(|e| format!("read {}: {e}", p.display()))?;
findings.suggested_fix: Omit the absolute path from IPC-facing error messages. Use only the filename component (p.file_name()) or a generic message like "conversation not found" for the returned Err string; log the full path internally with log::error! instead.

findings.title: Blocking std::process::Command::output() on async task thread during CLI path re-resolution
findings.description: resolve_claude_exe_uncached() calls std::process::Command::output() (spawns where.exe / which and waits), a blocking syscall that can take 100–500 ms. resolve_claude_exe() invokes it at line 209 on the slow path (cache miss or stale path), and resolve_claude_exe() is called by claude_command(), which is called from multiple async Tauri commands (assistant_enhance_prompt, assistant_send, etc.). This blocks the tokio worker thread for the duration of the subprocess wait — stalling all other tasks sharing that thread and risking executor starvation under load.
findings.evidence: let resolved = resolve_claude_exe_uncached();
findings.suggested_fix: Wrap the slow path in tokio::task::spawn_blocking or move the entire resolve_claude_exe call into spawn_blocking at the claude_command() call sites that are async. Alternatively, pre-resolve on app startup in a spawn_blocking call and cache atomically; async callers never hit the slow path at turn time.

findings.title: Blocking filesystem stat (is_file) held inside std::sync::Mutex on async task thread
findings.description: Inside resolve_claude_exe, the CLAUDE_EXE std::sync::Mutex guard is acquired at line 196 and held until the end of the inner block (line 207). While the guard is live, line 202 calls p.is_file(), which is a blocking stat() syscall. Any async task that calls claude_command() → resolve_claude_exe() holds this global Mutex while blocking the tokio worker thread on I/O. A second concurrent async call that also tries to acquire CLAUDE_EXE will park its thread trying to take the mutex, propagating the blockage across tasks.
findings.evidence: Some(p) if p.is_file() => return Some(p.clone()),
findings.suggested_fix: Clone the cached PathBuf while the lock is held (cheap, no I/O), drop the lock, then call is_file() outside the critical section. If the stat fails, proceed to the slow-path re-resolution. This eliminates blocking I/O under the mutex while preserving the invalidation logic.

findings.title: Negative CLI resolution cached forever — re-install not detected without restart
findings.description: When `resolve_claude_exe_uncached()` returns `None` (CLI not on PATH), the result is written into `CLAUDE_EXE` as `Some(None)` and the fast-path at line 203 short-circuits all future calls with an immediate `return None`. Unlike the stale-path arm (line 204, which falls through to re-resolve), the `None` arm is permanent for the process lifetime. A user who installs the Claude CLI after Rift starts will see 'CLI not found' on every spawn attempt until a full app restart, even though the fix the comment describes (re-stat to detect moves/removals) works correctly for the opposite direction.
findings.evidence: None => return None, // cached "no CLI on PATH"
findings.suggested_fix: Treat `None` the same as a stale path: fall through to re-resolve. Replace the `None =>` arm with `None => {}` so both stale-path and not-found cases drop to the slow-path re-resolution below. The re-resolution is cheap (one `where.exe` call) and only happens when the CLI is absent, which is not the hot path.

findings.title: Sidecar cleanup silently swallows remove_file errors — leaks .cwd/.model files on delete
findings.description: `delete_session_cwd` (line 492) and `delete_session_model` (line 530) both use `let _ = std::fs::remove_file(&p)` with no logging. If removal fails (permissions, file locked, I/O error), the caller receives no indication and the sidecar leaks. The leaked `.cwd` sidecar means a re-created conversation with the same CLI session UUID would pick up the old pinned cwd on resume, potentially routing turns to a stale workspace path. The save counterparts (`save_session_cwd`, `save_session_model`) both emit `log::warn!` on failure — the cleanup paths are inconsistent with this policy.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `log::warn!` on removal failure in both `delete_session_cwd` and `delete_session_model`, mirroring the save counterparts: `if let Err(e) = std::fs::remove_file(&p) { log::warn!("assistant: delete session cwd {}: {e}", p.display()); }`

findings.title: Unbounded message payload written to disk without size guard
findings.description: assistant_save_conversation accepts a Conversation struct from the Tauri IPC channel. The messages field is serde_json::Value — fully attacker-controlled, unbounded size. serde_json::to_string at line 601 serializes the whole value into an in-memory String with no length cap before writing to disk. A hostile renderer (or XSS in the WebView) can pass a multi-GB messages blob, causing OOM during serialization or disk exhaustion. No size check exists anywhere in the path before the write.
findings.suggested_fix: Before calling serde_json::to_string, check the serialized size or estimate the payload size from convo.messages. A simple guard such as checking the byte length of the messages JSON before serialization (e.g., refuse if the raw Value exceeds a threshold like 50 MB) would prevent unbounded allocation. Alternatively, use serde_json::to_writer with a size-counting writer wrapper that returns Err once a limit is exceeded.

findings.title: Workspace root paths joined with newline separator without stripping embedded newlines
findings.description:
write_mcp_config joins workspace roots into a single RIFT_MCP_ROOTS env-var string using newline as a delimiter (line 741: .join("
")). to_string_lossy() at line 739 does not strip embedded newlines from path components. On a POSIX host where a directory name can legally contain 
, a user-controlled workspace path like /workspace/foo
bar/baz would be split by the MCP server child into two roots — /workspace/foo and bar/baz — with bar/baz being an attacker-chosen relative path that bypasses the workspace-root boundary enforced by mcp_server.rs. Windows NTFS forbids newlines in paths so this
findings.suggested_fix: Strip or reject newlines from each path component before joining: replace \n and \r with a safe separator or return Err if any root contains a newline. Alternatively, switch RIFT_MCP_ROOTS to a JSON-encoded array (json!([...]) passed as a string) so the delimiter is structurally unambiguous regardless of path content.

findings.title: Blocking OS keychain + file I/O on async executor thread in assistant_auth_probe
findings.description: assistant_auth_probe is an async fn running on the Tokio executor. Lines 936-937 call load_config() (synchronous std::fs::read_to_string) and current_api_key() which calls crate::secrets::get() → keyring::Entry::get_password(), a blocking OS Credential Manager call (Windows). Blocking the executor thread stalls all other async tasks sharing that thread for the duration of the keychain round-trip, which can be tens to hundreds of milliseconds on a slow Credential Manager (e.g. roaming profiles, domain-joined machines).
findings.evidence:
let _cfg = load_config(); // run keychain migration / surface any stale legacy field
    out.api_key_configured = current_api_key().is_some();
findings.suggested_fix: Wrap both calls in tokio::task::spawn_blocking: `let api_key_configured = tokio::task::spawn_blocking(|| { let _ = load_config(); current_api_key().is_some() }).await.unwrap_or(false);` This moves the file I/O and keychain call off the async executor thread pool.

findings.title: Unprotected read-modify-write race on config.json across concurrent setter commands
findings.description: Every assistant_set_* command (lines 1077-1199, ~8 setters) follows the pattern: load_config() → mutate one field → save_config(). There is no mutex or lock guarding this read-modify-write cycle. If two setter commands run concurrently (e.g. assistant_set_max_budget_usd and assistant_set_thinking_effort), the second writer's load_config() reads the old value before the first writer has saved, and its subsequent save_config() overwrites the first writer's field silently. The tmp+rename in save_config() (line 687-689) prevents torn bytes on disk but does not prevent this lost-update. The code co
findings.suggested_fix: Add a static Mutex<()> (or Mutex<AssistantConfig> as a write-back cache) gating all config read-modify-write cycles: `static CONFIG_LOCK: Mutex<()> = Mutex::new(()); let _g = CONFIG_LOCK.lock().unwrap(); let mut cfg = load_config(); cfg.use_full_config = Some(value); save_config(&cfg)`. Alternatively, keep an in-memory Arc<Mutex<AssistantConfig>> as the authoritative state and only flush to disk within the lock.

findings.title: Silent swallow of chmod failure on MCP config file
findings.description: On Unix, the attempt to tighten permissions on the MCP config file (which holds a bridge token) uses `let _ = std::fs::set_permissions(...)`, silently discarding any error. If the chmod fails the file is left world-readable for the entire session lifetime, with no warning in the log. Violates fail-loud: a security-sensitive operation whose failure is never surfaced.
findings.evidence: let _ = std::fs::set_permissions(&path, std::fs::Permissions::from_mode(0o600));
findings.suggested_fix: Replace `let _ =` with an explicit match or `.unwrap_or_else`: `if let Err(e) = std::fs::set_permissions(&path, std::fs::Permissions::from_mode(0o600)) { log::warn!("assistant: failed to set 0600 on mcp-config {}: {e}", path.display()); }`. This preserves non-fatal behaviour while making the failure visible.

findings.title: Dead `full` trust-level variant tied to stripped RCON feature
findings.description: The `is_valid_trust_level` validator accepts `"full"`, and its doc comment says it is "reserved for RCON raw passthrough (phase 2)". RCON was fully stripped in the pure-assistant conversion (2026-06-03). The `"full"` variant is now unreachable in any real code path (no backend branch acts on it differently from `"standard"`), but it can still be written to config and passed to the MCP child via `RIFT_TRUST_LEVEL`, confusing the server-side trust gate with a value it may not handle.
findings.suggested_fix: Remove `"full"` from the `matches!` arms and update the doc comment. If a future escalated-trust tier is ever needed it can be re-added then with a real implementation behind it.

findings.title: Raw child stderr forwarded to IPC error string — can leak API key material
findings.description: When the child process exits non-zero, the complete raw stderr buffer is formatted directly into the Tauri command error string returned to the frontend (lines 1380-1385 for enhance, 1509-1515 for title, 1796-1801 for summarize). The subprocess is invoked with ANTHROPIC_API_KEY injected into its environment (line 1623). If the CLI emits the key value in its stderr (credential-error trace, debug output, '--bare' auth failures), the secret travels through the IPC boundary into the frontend and from there into any logging, analytics, or display layer. No scrubbing occurs before the format! call.
findings.evidence: format!("enhance failed: {msg}")  // msg = stderr_buf.trim(), child ran with cmd.env("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY", &k)
findings.suggested_fix: Before forwarding stderr to the IPC error, redact known-secret patterns: strip any line matching a known key prefix (e.g., 'sk-ant-') or apply a generic high-entropy token regex. At minimum, log the raw stderr internally (log::warn!) and return a generic 'child process error (see app log)' string to the frontend.

findings.title: I/O error on stdout silently terminates loop instead of propagating
findings.description: Both assistant_enhance_prompt (line 1337) and assistant_generate_title (line 1475) use `while let Ok(Some(line)) = lines.next_line().await`. The Err(_) arm is treated identically to Ok(None) (end of stream), so any I/O error on the stdout pipe silently breaks the loop. The accumulator is left with whatever was collected before the error, or empty. The function then surfaces this as 'enhancer returned empty output' / 'title generation returned empty output' — the real I/O error is never reported. This violates fail-loud: an OS-level read error becomes a misleading empty-output error.
findings.evidence: while let Ok(Some(line)) = lines.next_line().await {
findings.suggested_fix: Change to a match or propagate errors: `while let Some(line) = lines.next_line().await.map_err(|e| format!("read stdout: {e}"))? { ... }`. This surfaces I/O errors immediately rather than silently falling through to the empty-output check.

findings.title: stdout_task panic silently swallowed via unwrap_or_default
findings.description: The summarize stdout task JoinHandle is awaited with `.unwrap_or_default()`. If the spawned task panics, the JoinError is silently discarded and the tuple defaults to (empty_string, 0.0, 0, 0, 0, 0, None). The empty `summary` then triggers `Err("summarize call returned empty text")` with no indication that a panic occurred. This masks real bugs. The sibling `stderr_task` on line 1791 correctly logs the panic via `unwrap_or_else`; the stdout task should match that pattern.
findings.evidence: stdout_task.await.unwrap_or_default();
findings.suggested_fix: Replace with `.unwrap_or_else(|e| { log::error!("summarize stdout drain task panicked: {e}"); Default::default() })` to surface the JoinError, matching the stderr_task pattern on line 1791.

findings.title: Blocking std::fs I/O inside async fn assistant_send
findings.description: assistant_send is an async Tauri command. Before spawning the child process it calls load_config() (std::fs::read_to_string), current_api_key() (calls load_config() again), load_session_cwd() (std::fs::read_to_string), save_session_cwd() (std::fs::write), load_session_model() (std::fs::read_to_string), save_session_model() (std::fs::write), and write_mcp_config() (more fs writes) -- all synchronous blocking filesystem calls directly on the tokio worker thread. Under normal local disk this stalls the worker for microseconds, but on a network drive, slow antivirus scan, or disk under load each c
findings.evidence:
let cfg = load_config();
    let api_key = current_api_key();
findings.suggested_fix: Wrap the pre-spawn setup block in tokio::task::spawn_blocking, or switch each helper to an async variant using tokio::fs::read_to_string / tokio::fs::write. Alternatively batch all reads into a single spawn_blocking closure that returns the needed values, then use them in the async context.

findings.title: Swallowed JoinError in summarize stdout task
findings.description: stdout_task.await.unwrap_or_default() silently discards a JoinError (task panic). The panic reason is lost; execution continues with a zeroed-out tuple. The blank summary is caught later at line 1804 as 'summarize call returned empty text', masking the real cause. The stderr task on line 1791 correctly logs and surfaces its JoinError, but stdout does not.
findings.evidence:
let (summary, cost_usd, input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_read, cache_create, result_model) =
        stdout_task.await.unwrap_or_default();
findings.suggested_fix: Mirror the stderr pattern: stdout_task.await.unwrap_or_else(|e| { log::error!("summarize stdout drain task panicked: {e}"); Default::default() }) — or propagate via `?` after mapping the JoinError to a string, so the caller sees the panic message.

findings.title: Dead SAFE_MCP entries reference stripped sync tools
findings.description: SAFE_MCP includes mcp__rift__sync_status, mcp__rift__drift_snapshot, and mcp__rift__reconcile_preview — all from the SFTP/sync half that was fully stripped in the pure-assistant conversion (2026-06-03). These tool names are never registered by mcp_server.rs, so they are permanently inert entries in the CLI allowlist. This is leftover dead code from the rip.
findings.evidence: const SAFE_MCP: &str = "mcp__rift__read_file,mcp__rift__list_dir,mcp__rift__grep,mcp__rift__sync_status,mcp__rift__drift_snapshot,mcp__rift__reconcile_preview,mcp__rift__ask_user";
findings.suggested_fix: Remove mcp__rift__sync_status, mcp__rift__drift_snapshot, and mcp__rift__reconcile_preview from SAFE_MCP. The live set is: mcp__rift__read_file, mcp__rift__list_dir, mcp__rift__grep, mcp__rift__ask_user.

findings.title: Panic on non-ASCII stderr: `buf[STDERR_TRIM..]` may slice mid-char-boundary
findings.description: When the stderr buffer exceeds STDERR_CAP (64 KiB), the trim path does `buf[STDERR_TRIM..]` where STDERR_TRIM = 32768 (a fixed byte offset). If any multi-byte UTF-8 sequence (non-ASCII locale message, emoji, Unicode path) straddles byte 32768, Rust panics with 'byte index N is not a char boundary'. The comment on the line below ('newline is always one [char boundary]') only applies to the `drain` cut point, not to this slice. The panic is caught by the `tokio::spawn` task boundary and surfaces as a `JoinError` at line 2836, silently discarding stderr content — but still constitutes an avoidabl
findings.evidence:
let cut = buf[STDERR_TRIM..]
    .find('\n')
    .map(|n| STDERR_TRIM + n + 1)
    .unwrap_or(STDERR_TRIM);
findings.suggested_fix: Replace `buf[STDERR_TRIM..]` with a char-boundary-safe slice: use `buf.char_indices().map(|(i,_)| i).filter(|&i| i >= STDERR_TRIM).next().unwrap_or(STDERR_TRIM)` to find the first valid char boundary at or after STDERR_TRIM before slicing. Or use `as_bytes()` + `find` on the byte slice, then verify the result is a char boundary via `buf.is_char_boundary(cut)`.

findings.title: Raw stderr from child process leaked to frontend via Tauri event and Err return
findings.description: The fallthrough error branch (non-empty stderr that isn't a 401) emits the full raw stderr string directly into a Tauri ERROR_EVENT (broadcast to all frontend listeners) and returns it as the Err(msg) string over the IPC boundary. The Claude CLI stderr can contain environment variable dumps (e.g. from startup errors showing the process env), partial credential strings, MCP server crash output with workspace paths, or OS locale-specific diagnostics. The 401-specific branch deliberately suppresses raw stderr and substitutes a safe message — the same treatment should apply to all non-empty stderr
findings.suggested_fix: Scrub or truncate `raw` before embedding: redact any token matching `sk-ant-[A-Za-z0-9-]+` and `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=\S+` with `[REDACTED]`, cap the embedded excerpt to ~500 chars, and log the full raw value at DEBUG level locally only. Alternatively, emit a fixed 'claude exited with N — see logs' message to the frontend and keep raw in the local log only.

findings.title: Blocking std::process::Command::status() inside async fn assistant_stop
findings.description: assistant_stop is an async Tauri command. On Windows (line 2971) it calls std::process::Command::new("taskkill").status(), and on Unix (line 2986) std::process::Command::new("kill").status(). Both .status() calls block the calling thread until the spawned process exits. On a Tokio work-stealing runtime this starves the thread for the duration of taskkill/kill execution, and under concurrent Stop requests can exhaust the thread pool. The fix is tokio::process::Command or tokio::task::spawn_blocking.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace std::process::Command with tokio::process::Command and .await its .status(), or wrap in tokio::task::spawn_blocking(|| ...).await. Both paths (Windows taskkill + Unix kill) need the same treatment.

findings.title: SAFE_MCP allowlist contains four stripped tools (dead post-conversion refs)
findings.description: The SAFE_MCP constant includes mcp__rift__sync_status, mcp__rift__drift_snapshot, mcp__rift__reconcile_preview, and mcp__rift__ask_user — tools that were ripped out during the pure-assistant conversion (2026-06-03). None of these names appear anywhere in mcp_server.rs. They are passed verbatim as --allowed-tools to the CLI in the prompting_mode branch. While the CLI ignores allowlist entries for nonexistent tools (so there is no runtime crash), the entries are dead references that mislead anyone reading the permission model and could mask a real gap if a future tool is added with a colliding n
findings.evidence: const SAFE_MCP: &str = "mcp__rift__read_file,mcp__rift__list_dir,mcp__rift__grep,mcp__rift__sync_status,mcp__rift__drift_snapshot,mcp__rift__reconcile_preview,mcp__rift__ask_user";
findings.suggested_fix: Remove the four stripped names. Correct value: "mcp__rift__read_file,mcp__rift__list_dir,mcp__rift__grep". Also drop the GIT_READ_MCP omission comment that still mentions ask_user if it references the now-gone remote-shell surface.

findings.title: Unreachable None arm in status match emits false error event
findings.description: The match at line 2856 has a None arm (lines 2858-2864) that emits an ERROR_EVENT and returns Err. The comment on line 2855 correctly notes `status` is always Some on this path — the only `break None` in the wait loop (line 2802) is gated on `result_seen == true`, and the guard at line 2850 returns Ok(()) before this match is reached whenever result_seen is true. The None arm is therefore unreachable dead code. If a future refactor makes it reachable, the user would receive a spurious error event for a turn that already succeeded.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace with `let status = status.expect("status is always Some when result_seen is false — invariant violated");` to document the invariant and panic loudly if it's ever broken rather than silently emitting a false error event.

findings.title: Claude CLI stderr logged verbatim — can contain auth tokens or OAuth secrets
findings.description: On non-zero exit the full stderr of the claude subprocess is captured and passed to log::warn! without scrubbing. Claude Code CLI writes OAuth flow details, bearer-token refresh errors, and occasionally the token value itself to stderr when auth fails. Application logs (written to disk and potentially forwarded via LogForwarder/DiagBus) will capture these verbatim. Any log sink that persists or transmits app logs (crash reporters, diagnostic uploads) receives the credential material.
findings.suggested_fix: Truncate and redact the stderr snippet before logging: cap to ~200 chars and strip any substring matching bearer/token/key patterns, or simply log only the exit status code without stderr content (the error path already returns the raw transcript, so the full stderr is not needed for user-facing diagnostics).

findings.title: FinalPayload.cleaned flag is wrong when scrubbed output is empty
findings.description: The `cleaned` field in `FinalPayload` is set to `active.cleanup_enabled`, but cleanup is only *attempted* when both `cleanup_enabled && !scrubbed.is_empty()` (line 483). When `scrubbed` is empty and `cleanup_enabled` is true, the code falls to the else branch returning `scrubbed.clone()` (empty string) — no cleanup ran — yet the frontend receives `cleaned: true`. The frontend likely uses this flag to annotate or post-process the result, so the lie corrupts that logic.
findings.evidence: cleaned: active.cleanup_enabled,
findings.suggested_fix: Track whether cleanup actually ran: `let (final_text, did_clean) = if active.cleanup_enabled && !scrubbed.is_empty() { ... (t, true) / (scrubbed.clone(), false) } else { (scrubbed.clone(), false) };` then emit `cleaned: did_clean`.

findings.title: load_config silently swallows all I/O errors — no log for unexpected failures
findings.description: `Err(_) => return SttConfig::default()` discards the error entirely with no log. A missing file (ENOENT) is expected, but permission-denied, disk errors, or other unexpected OS failures are silently masked by falling back to defaults. The user gets defaults with zero indication that their saved config was unreadable.
findings.evidence: Err(_) => return SttConfig::default(),
findings.suggested_fix: Match on the error kind: `Err(e) if e.kind() == std::io::ErrorKind::NotFound => return SttConfig::default(), Err(e) => { log::warn!("stt-config read failed ({e}), using defaults"); return SttConfig::default(); }`

findings.title: Download error silently replaced by cleanup-lock error
findings.description: After `model_manager::download` completes (success or failure), the post-download cleanup block re-acquires the mutex at line 604 with `?`. If the mutex is poisoned at that point (e.g. a prior panic in another thread holding the lock), the `?` operator causes an early return of `Err("cancel slot lock: {e}")`, discarding whatever `res` contained — including the actual download error. The caller receives the wrong error and has no way to distinguish a lock-poison event from a real download failure. Additionally, on success the slot is left non-None if this branch is taken, so a stale cancel hand
findings.suggested_fix: Use `if let Ok(mut slot) = state.0.lock() { *slot = None; }` (ignore cleanup errors rather than masking `res`), then unconditionally `return res;`. This matches the intent: slot cleanup is best-effort; the caller must always see the true download result.

findings.title: `--permission-mode bypassPermissions` passed to every claude subprocess spawned for transcript cleanup
findings.description: `stt_clean_transcript` (line 624-627) delegates to `cleanup::polish`, which spawns `claude -p --permission-mode bypassPermissions` (cleanup.rs line 59). The `bypassPermissions` flag instructs the Claude CLI to suppress all permission prompts and allow any file/tool operation the model requests. Because the system prompt and user content (raw transcript) are both runtime-controllable strings (the transcript comes from Whisper/microphone input and is passed verbatim as stdin), a prompt-injection in the transcript could direct the subprocess to perform file reads, writes, or shell commands with n

cmd.arg("-p")
        .arg("--model")
        .arg(HAIKU_MODEL)
        .arg("--permission-mode")
        .arg("bypassPermissions")
findings.suggested_fix: Remove `--permission-mode bypassPermissions`. The `--print` (`-p`) mode with `--model` does not need elevated permissions for text-in/text-out transcript cleanup. If certain tool permissions are genuinely required, use `--allowedTools` to whitelist only the exact tools needed rather than bypassing all permission checks.

findings.title: tool_grep: TOCTOU between binary probe and full read — double open of same path
findings.description: The binary probe opens the file (line 278), reads 8 KiB, then drops the handle at the end of the inner block (line 285). A second std::fs::open happens implicitly inside std::fs::read(p) at line 286. Between the two opens, the file can be replaced, truncated, or deleted. On Windows this window is narrow due to file locking, but on a busy workspace the second read may see different content or fail. Additionally, two OS file-handle allocations are used when one would suffice.
findings.suggested_fix: Keep the File open from the probe phase: after the probe passes, seek(SeekFrom::Start(0)) and read the remainder (up to a size cap) from the same handle. This eliminates the TOCTOU window and halves the number of open() syscalls per scanned file.

findings.title: tool_grep: off-by-one lets one extra file scan past MAX_GREP_FILES
findings.description: files_scanned is incremented at line 290, then checked with `>` (strictly-greater) at line 291. This means the loop body fully executes for file number MAX_GREP_FILES+1 (5001) — reads it, UTF-8 decodes it, runs the regex on it — before breaking. The guard should use `>=` (check before processing) or the increment should move to before the guard.
findings.evidence:
files_scanned += 1;
        if files_scanned > MAX_GREP_FILES {

findings.title: fields (serde_json::Value) forwarded to frontend without scrubbing
findings.description: emit_with_fields accepts an arbitrary serde_json::Value and publish() forwards event.fields to the frontend bus unchanged. Scrubbing in publish() covers only event.message and event.file. Any caller that embeds an absolute path, homedir prefix, auth token, or error message containing credentials in fields bypasses scrub_log_message entirely. The 58-site comment at line 169 acknowledges this class of bypass existed for direct emit* calls; fields is another such bypass.
findings.suggested_fix: In publish(), walk the fields JSON value and apply scrub_log_message to every String leaf before broadcasting. A helper like `scrub_json_strings(v: &mut serde_json::Value)` that recurses into objects/arrays and replaces string values via scrub_log_message covers both existing and future field embeddings.

findings.title: Blocking std::sync::Mutex locked inside async task
findings.description: The spawn_frontend_pump async task calls log::warn!() on RecvError::Lagged. That macro routes through LogForwarder::log() → bus().publish() → self.recent.lock() (line 189), which is a std::sync::Mutex::lock() — a blocking OS primitive. Holding or acquiring a blocking std mutex inside a tokio async task starves the executor thread for the duration of the lock, and can deadlock if another task on the same thread holds the lock while awaiting. The concrete call chain is: async loop recv (line 430) → Lagged branch (line 476) → log::warn! (line 481) → LogForwarder::log (line 381) → bus().publish()
findings.suggested_fix: Replace std::sync::Mutex with tokio::sync::Mutex for DiagBus::recent and make publish() async, OR use try_lock() with a fallback skip on contention (acceptable for the ring buffer), OR move the log::warn! call outside any code path that re-enters publish() — e.g. emit a DiagEvent directly via tx.send() without touching the ring buffer from inside the async loop.

findings.title: JoinHandle from spawn_frontend_pump discarded — task leaks on teardown
findings.description: tauri::async_runtime::spawn() returns a JoinHandle that is immediately dropped (not stored, not awaited, not aborted). The loop inside runs forever (Closed branch is the only exit). On app teardown there is no mechanism to signal the task to stop or to wait for it to finish, meaning the task and its broadcast Receiver remain alive past logical shutdown. If the tauri AppHandle is dropped before the task exits, subsequent app.emit() calls (line 474) will silently fail or panic depending on the tauri version, and the Receiver keeps the broadcast channel's slot count non-zero indefinitely.
findings.suggested_fix: Return the JoinHandle from spawn_frontend_pump (change return type to JoinHandle<()>) and store it in AppState or a global abort registration. Alternatively accept a CancellationToken and select! on it inside the loop, then call token.cancel() during the Tauri on_exit handler.

findings.title: Silently swallowed app.emit error in frontend pump
findings.description: app.emit() returns a Result but the error is discarded with `let _ = ...`. If the webview is closed, the IPC channel errors, or serialization fails, the pump loop continues silently with no log entry. The frontend silently stops receiving diag events with no observable trace — violates the project's fail-loud rule.
findings.evidence: let _ = app.emit("diag://event", &ev);
findings.suggested_fix: Replace with `if let Err(e) = app.emit("diag://event", &ev) { log::warn!("diag emit error: {e}"); }` so failures surface in the log forwarder and activity feed.

Only DiagStage::System, DiagStage::Log, DriftScanStart, and DriftScanResult are actually emitted by live code. The dead variants inflate the serialized enum surface sent to the frontend and keep the is_criti

findings.title: current_branch() output used as git arg without validate_ref
findings.description: tool_git_push falls back to current_branch(root) when no branch arg is supplied (line 347), then passes the raw trimmed stdout directly into run_git as the branch arg (line 353). The module's own security contract (§11) states all string params must be validated before reaching Command, but this path skips validate_ref entirely. Since Command::new/args is used (no shell), classic shell injection is not possible, but a branch name starting with '-' (e.g. '--upload-pack=evil' set by a malicious repo's HEAD) would reach git as a flag. The existing validate_ref allowlist blocks exactly this class
findings.suggested_fix: Pipe the current_branch result through validate_ref before use: `None => validate_ref("branch", &current_branch(root)?)?`

findings.title: Raw git stderr surfaced in errors may leak credential fragments
findings.description: err_text() (line 122-129) returns git's raw stderr (or stdout) trimmed and forwarded as the error message string. git can include partial HTTPS credential info, PAT fragments embedded in remote URLs (e.g. 'fatal: Authentication failed for https://user:TOKEN@github.com/...'), or SSH key paths in error messages. These propagate through all tool_git_* callers (e.g. line 284, 330, 355) into MCP responses visible to the Claude model context and any logging that records tool errors.
findings.suggested_fix: Scrub URLs containing credentials before returning: apply a regex like `https?://[^@]*@` → `https://<redacted>@` on the error string, or limit stderr forwarding to a fixed byte cap (e.g. 512 bytes) and strip lines matching credential patterns.

findings.title: Unbounded stdout buffer in run_git — full diff collected before truncation check
findings.description: tool_git_diff truncates output at MAX_DIFF_BYTES (64 KB) AFTER cmd.output() has already buffered the entire diff into a Vec<u8> in RAM. On a workspace with large generated files, binary assets, or a lock-file change, git diff can produce hundreds of MB or more. The truncation check on line 243 arrives too late — the process has already OOM-pressured the MCP child. The same pattern affects git_log if the repo has an enormous history (less likely but same code path).
findings.evidence: if out.stdout.len() > MAX_DIFF_BYTES {
findings.suggested_fix: Pass git a byte-budget at invocation time: add --diff-filter=ACMRT and a byte-limit via git diff --stat first, or use -U0 combined with passing the limit as a git option (e.g. core.bigFileThreshold). The simplest safe fix is to pipe through head -c <MAX_DIFF_BYTES+margin> using Command piping instead of collecting the full output, or use cmd.stdout(Stdio::piped()) + manual incremental read that stops after MAX_DIFF_BYTES bytes, killing the child before it produces more.

findings.title: Dead unreachable early-return in `tool_git_status` masks clean-tree logic
findings.description: `git status --porcelain=v1 -b` always emits at least one line (the `## <branch>` header) when the command succeeds. The `lines.is_empty()` guard at line 194 can therefore never be true after `out.ok()` passes, making the "Working tree clean." return at line 195 dead code.
